messages.content: My report script uses the REPORT_DIR environment variable when I run it from my shell, and the reports land in /srv/reports like they should. The same script runs from our scheduler at night and the reports end up in ./reports instead. Same code, same machine. What's different?

arguments.code:
import os, subprocess, sys

PROG = (
    "import os\n"
    "print('REPORT_DIR =', os.environ.get('REPORT_DIR', '<unset> -> ./reports'))\n"
)

shell_env = dict(os.environ, REPORT_DIR="/srv/reports")
sched_env = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"]}

for label, env in (("interactive shell", shell_env), ("scheduler", sched_env)):
    out = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", PROG], env=env,
                         capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(label + ":", out.stdout.strip())

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
interactive shell: REPORT_DIR = /srv/reports
scheduler: REPORT_DIR = <unset> -> ./reports

The code is identical; the environment it inherits is not. Your interactive shell has REPORT_DIR exported, so the program sees /srv/reports. The scheduler starts the job with a nearly empty environment — here just PATH — so the variable is absent and the program silently falls back to its default, ./reports.

This is the single most common shape of 'works on my machine': a program reading configuration from its surroundings, and the surroundings differing by launcher. Shells accumulate variables from your profile, your session, your exports. Schedulers, cron, and service managers start from a deliberately minimal set.

Fix at the deployment layer, not the code layer: set REPORT_DIR explicitly in the scheduler's job definition (or the service unit), the same place the schedule itself is defined. And as a defensive habit, have long-running jobs log their effective configuration at startup, so the next time the output lands somewhere unexpected, the log says which value the process actually ran with.

I set DATABASE_URL in the service's environment file to our Postgres server, restarted, and the app still quietly uses a local sqlite file. No error anywhere. The variable is definitely in the file — I can see it. What am I missing?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
program connected with: sqlite:///local.db
set in the environment:  ['DATABSE_URL']

The variable is in the file, but under the wrong name: the environment defines DATABSE_URL — one transposed pair of letters — while the program reads DATABASE_URL. The lookup misses, and because the code supplies a default (sqlite:///local.db), the miss is silent. No error is exactly what a fallback default produces.

Typos in variable names are nastier than typos in code: code typos usually fail loudly at parse or lookup time, but an environment is just a bag of strings — nothing ever complains that a key exists which nobody reads, or that a read key was never set.

Forensics that catch this class: dump the effective environment (sorted) and eyeball it against the list of names the program actually reads, or grep the environment for near-misses of the expected name. Prevention: fail fast on startup for required variables — read them with a lookup that raises when absent instead of a default that hides the absence, and reserve silent defaults for values that are genuinely optional.

Our deploy tooling sets CACHE_DIR to an empty string on the staging box to mean 'no special cache dir', and my Python code does os.environ.get('CACHE_DIR', '/tmp/cache'). A teammate says empty and unset are the same thing here. Are they?

arguments.code:
import os

os.environ.pop("CACHE_DIR", None)
print("unset:        get ->", repr(os.environ.get("CACHE_DIR", "<default>")))

os.environ["CACHE_DIR"] = ""
print("set to empty: get ->", repr(os.environ.get("CACHE_DIR", "<default>")))
print("empty falls through 'or' like unset:", repr(os.environ.get("CACHE_DIR") or "/tmp/cache"))
print("'in' can still tell them apart:", "CACHE_DIR" in os.environ)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
unset:        get -> '<default>'
set to empty: get -> ''
empty falls through 'or' like unset: '/tmp/cache'
'in' can still tell them apart: True

They are not the same, and the run shows the seam. When CACHE_DIR is unset, .get returns your default. When it is set to an empty string, .get returns the empty string — the default never applies, because from the environment's point of view the variable exists. Code downstream then tries to use '' as a path, which typically means 'the current directory' or a confusing relative path, not '/tmp/cache'.

The third line shows why the confusion survives: `os.environ.get('CACHE_DIR') or '/tmp/cache'` treats empty and unset identically, because '' is falsy. So one idiom distinguishes them and the other doesn't — two parts of a codebase can disagree about what the staging box is configured to do.

Decide which meaning you intend and write it explicitly. If empty should mean 'use the default', normalize once at startup: `cache_dir = os.environ.get('CACHE_DIR') or '/tmp/cache'`, and document that empty means unset. If empty is a real, distinct instruction (for example 'disable caching'), test membership with `'CACHE_DIR' in os.environ` and handle the empty case on purpose. The bug is never the empty string itself; it's two readers interpreting it differently.

I moved a working shell script into cron and it fails with errors about commands and files that all exist. My shell has a big environment — aliases, exports, the lot. What does cron actually give my script to work with?

Almost nothing, and that's by design. A typical cron implementation starts each job with a small, fixed environment: a short PATH (often just /usr/bin:/bin), HOME set to your home directory, SHELL=/bin/sh, and your username variables — and none of the exports, aliases, or functions from your interactive shell. Aliases and functions don't exist at all outside your interactive shell config; exported variables exist only if cron's own configuration or the crontab itself sets them.

So a script that relies on a PATH your profile built up, a variable your .bashrc exports, or a tool you always invoke by a nickname will fail under cron while looking perfectly healthy interactively. The commands and files 'all exist' — from your shell's vantage point. From the job's vantage point, some of them genuinely aren't reachable.

The working rules: in anything a scheduler will run, use absolute paths for commands and files (or set PATH explicitly at the top of the script), set every variable the script needs inside the script or the crontab, and never let correctness depend on your interactive environment. When a cron job misbehaves, reproduce it with a minimal environment — `env -i /bin/sh -c '...'` gets you much closer to what cron sees than rerunning it from your shell.

Our app runs under systemd. I exported APP_REGION in my SSH session and restarted the service, but it still reports the old region. A colleague says systemd doesn't care about my shell. What actually feeds a service its environment?

Your colleague is right. A systemd service does not inherit anything from the shell you happen to be logged into — not your exports, not your profile, not the environment of the terminal where you typed systemctl restart. The service manager builds the process environment from its own configuration.

The sources, in the order systemd assembles them: a small built-in default (including a fixed PATH), variables set with Environment= lines in the unit file, and variables loaded from files named by EnvironmentFile= directives. Later sources override earlier ones. You can inspect the result with `systemctl show <service> -p Environment` and edit it with `systemctl edit` (a drop-in override) followed by a daemon-reload and restart.

Two traps follow. First, an EnvironmentFile that doesn't exist makes the service fail to start unless the path is prefixed with a dash to mark it optional — a classic 'worked before I touched it' outage. Second, editing your shell's environment and restarting feels like it should work, because on a developer laptop the shell and the app are loosely the same world. Under a service manager they are separate worlds that only meet through the unit file.

So: put APP_REGION in the unit or its drop-in, reload, restart, and verify with systemctl show rather than by trusting the restart.

In my Python service I changed APP_TIMEOUT in the environment and restarted nothing else — the running code kept using the old timeout, but a helper function in the same file picked up the new value immediately. How can both be true?

arguments.code:
import os

os.environ["APP_TIMEOUT"] = "30"
SETTINGS = {"timeout": int(os.environ["APP_TIMEOUT"])}  # read once, at import

os.environ["APP_TIMEOUT"] = "60"  # the environment changes afterwards

def live_timeout():
    return int(os.environ["APP_TIMEOUT"])

print("module constant (import time):", SETTINGS["timeout"])
print("function reading live env:    ", live_timeout())

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
module constant (import time): 30
function reading live env:     60

Both are true because the two readers read at different times. The module-level SETTINGS dict was built once, when the module was first imported, and it captured the value 30 as a plain integer. Changing os.environ afterwards changes the environment mapping, but nothing reaches back into the already-built dict. The helper function, by contrast, performs its os.environ lookup on every call, so it sees 60 immediately.

This split — snapshot at import versus lookup at call time — explains a lot of confusing partial behavior after a config change: some knobs respond, others don't, depending on where each was read. It's also why 'I changed the variable and restarted nothing' is an underspecified report; the question is always which reads happened after the change.

Decide deliberately which behavior each setting gets. Values that must be consistent for the process's lifetime (ports, connection targets) are fine read once at startup — and then a restart is the honest way to change them. Values meant to be tunable at runtime should be read at use time, or through an explicit reload path. The defect is the accidental mixture, where the author never chose.

In my bash script I set TOKEN=abc123 at the top, and a Python helper the script calls can't see it. If I type the same lines in my terminal the helper sees it fine after a while. Why does the child process not get my variable?

arguments.code:
TOKEN=abc123
echo "before export, child sees: $(python3 -c 'import os; print(os.environ.get("TOKEN", "<missing>"))')"
export TOKEN
echo "after export,  child sees: $(python3 -c 'import os; print(os.environ.get("TOKEN", "<missing>"))')"

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
before export, child sees: <missing>
after export,  child sees: abc123

A shell variable and an environment variable are different things that share a syntax. `TOKEN=abc123` creates a variable inside the shell process only. Child processes inherit the shell's *environment* — the subset of variables marked for export — and an unexported variable is simply not in that subset, so the Python helper's os.environ has no TOKEN in it.

`export TOKEN` flips the export attribute on the existing variable, and from then on every child the shell launches receives it. That's also why it 'works after a while' in your terminal: at some point in an interactive session you (or a profile script, or a tool like direnv) exported it, and the terminal keeps that state invisibly.

Two corollaries worth keeping. First, exporting is one-directional and one-generation deep in effect: a child can never modify its parent's environment, so a helper script that 'sets up' variables for the caller only works if it's sourced, not executed. Second, in scripts, export what you set if anything downstream needs it — or better, pass values to helpers as arguments, which makes the dependency visible instead of ambient.

A setup guide told me to set a variable called Path on our Linux server and the app still didn't find anything. On my Windows laptop at home, Path is definitely a thing. Is this an operating system difference?

Yes — variable names are case-sensitive on Linux and case-insensitive on Windows, and that difference bites exactly here. On Linux, PATH and Path are two unrelated variables; your app (and the shell's command lookup) reads PATH, so a carefully set Path sits there unused while everything behaves as if you set nothing. On Windows, the environment treats names case-insensitively, so Path, PATH, and path all refer to the same variable, which is why the guide's spelling worked at home.

The same caution applies to your own application variables: APP_HOME and App_Home are distinct on Linux. Conventions exist partly to prevent this — environment variables are written in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE almost everywhere, and matching the convention makes a mis-cased name visually obvious.

Forensic tip: when a variable 'is set' but has no effect, dump the environment sorted (`env | sort` or `printenv`) and read the names character by character rather than trusting your memory of what you typed. The bug is nearly always visible in the dump once you look at the spelling instead of the intention.
I control debug mode with APP_DEBUG in the environment and check it with bool(os.environ.get('APP_DEBUG')) in Python. Ops set APP_DEBUG=false for production and debug output got MORE verbose. Why?

arguments.code:
import os

for raw in ("false", "0", "no", "true"):
    os.environ["APP_DEBUG"] = raw
    naive = bool(os.environ["APP_DEBUG"])
    parsed = os.environ["APP_DEBUG"].lower() in ("1", "true", "yes", "on")
    print(f"APP_DEBUG={raw!r:8} bool(value) -> {naive!s:5} parsed -> {parsed}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
APP_DEBUG='false'  bool(value) -> True  parsed -> False
APP_DEBUG='0'      bool(value) -> True  parsed -> False
APP_DEBUG='no'     bool(value) -> True  parsed -> False
APP_DEBUG='true'   bool(value) -> True  parsed -> True

Because environment variables are strings, and in Python every non-empty string is truthy — including 'false', '0', and 'no'. bool() on the value answers the question 'is there a non-empty string here?', not 'did the human mean yes?'. Ops set APP_DEBUG=false, the string is non-empty, bool() returns True, and debug mode turned on. The run shows the same trap for '0' and 'no'.

The parsed column is the fix: compare the string, case-insensitively, against an explicit set of affirmative spellings and treat everything else as off. Pick the accepted spellings deliberately ({'1','true','yes','on'} is a common set) and document them, because the next person will guess — and different tools guess differently, which is how one service reads 'false' as off while its neighbor reads it as on.

The general principle: every value that arrives from the environment, a file, or the network is text, and it stays text until your code parses it into a type. Bugs like this one live in the gap between the type the human meant and the type the code assumed.

When a bug is 'works on my machine, fails on yours', my instinct is to diff the code and the inputs. A senior engineer told me to diff the environments first. What does that actually look like in practice?

It means capturing, from both machines, the facts about the surroundings the program runs in, and comparing those before suspecting the code — because identical code in different surroundings is the usual story. Concretely, capture: the interpreter/runtime version, the versions of the libraries actually imported, the relevant environment variables (names and values, sorted), the working directory, the PATH and what it resolves your commands to, the user the process runs as, and the machine timezone and locale.

Then diff the two captures. `env | sort` on both sides and a literal diff of the outputs resolves a surprising fraction of these bugs in minutes: a variable present on one side, a PATH entry order flipped, a LANG difference. The senior engineer isn't being mystical — code is usually identical because it came from the same repo, while environments are assembled by hand, by installers, by profiles, by history, and they drift.

Make it a habit to produce this capture as a single artifact — a small manifest printed by the program itself at startup, or a script that prints versions, sorted env keys, cwd, and PATH — and attach it to bug reports. 'Works on my machine' stops being an argument the moment both machines have to state, in writing, what they actually are.

There are two different `deploy` scripts on our build box, in two different tool directories. Sometimes we get the old behavior, sometimes the new, and people swear it changed on its own. Nothing is being edited. What decides which one runs?

arguments.code:
import os, shutil, subprocess, tempfile

root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for label in ("alpha", "beta"):
    d = os.path.join(root, label)
    os.makedirs(d)
    p = os.path.join(d, "deploy")
    with open(p, "w") as f:
        f.write(f"#!/bin/sh\necho deploy-from-{label}\n")
    os.chmod(p, 0o755)

for order in (("alpha", "beta"), ("beta", "alpha")):
    path = os.pathsep.join(os.path.join(root, d) for d in order)
    found = shutil.which("deploy", path=path)
    print("PATH order", order, "-> runs", os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(found)))
    out = subprocess.run([found], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print("   output:", out.stdout.strip())

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
PATH order ('alpha', 'beta') -> runs alpha
   output: deploy-from-alpha
PATH order ('beta', 'alpha') -> runs beta
   output: deploy-from-beta

PATH order decides, and PATH order is environment — it can differ between shells, users, schedulers, and sessions on the same box without anyone editing either script. The shell (and shutil.which, which mirrors it) walks the PATH entries left to right and takes the first directory containing an executable of that name. Whichever of alpha or beta appears first wins, completely and silently.

So 'it changed on its own' usually means the PATH changed: a profile edit, a tool installer prepending its directory, a different account running the job, a scheduler's minimal PATH. The scripts were never ambiguous; the resolution context was.

Forensics: `which deploy` (or `type -a deploy` to see every match in order) in the exact context that misbehaved — not in your shell, if your shell isn't where it failed. Prevention for anything that matters: call the intended script by absolute path, and treat two same-named tools on one box as a naming bug waiting for a PATH shuffle to expose it.

Our nightly backup job fails with 'zzbackup: command not found' when the scheduler runs it, but I can run the exact same command line from my shell and it works. The tool is installed — I use it all the time. Reproduce what's happening and explain it.

arguments.code:
import os, shutil, tempfile

root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
tools = os.path.join(root, "tools")
os.makedirs(tools)
p = os.path.join(tools, "zzbackup")
with open(p, "w") as f:
    f.write("#!/bin/sh\necho backup ran\n")
os.chmod(p, 0o755)

interactive = tools + os.pathsep + "/usr/bin:/bin"
scheduler = "/usr/bin:/bin"
print("interactive PATH finds zzbackup:", shutil.which("zzbackup", path=interactive) is not None)
print("scheduler   PATH finds zzbackup:", shutil.which("zzbackup", path=scheduler) is not None)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
interactive PATH finds zzbackup: True
scheduler   PATH finds zzbackup: False

The tool is installed — in a directory that only your shell's PATH knows about. Your interactive PATH includes the tools directory (your profile put it there), so the name resolves. The scheduler runs the job with a short, fixed PATH of /usr/bin:/bin; the tools directory is not in it, the lookup fails, and the shell reports 'command not found' — a message about the search, not about the tool's existence.

This is why 'command not found' from a scheduled job should never send you checking whether the tool is installed. Check instead: which directories does this job's PATH contain, and is the tool's directory among them? `which zzbackup` answers for your shell only; the job's environment is a different one.

Fixes, in order of robustness: invoke the tool by absolute path in the job definition; or set PATH explicitly at the top of the job/script to include the tools directory; or install the tool into a standard location that's on every PATH. What not to do is copy your whole interactive PATH into the job — it drags in directories that exist for your session's convenience and makes the job depend on them silently.

My data loader opens 'data/input.csv' with a relative path. It works when I run it from the project folder, and fails with FileNotFoundError when our task runner launches it. The file is right there in the project. Why does the same relative path behave differently?

arguments.code:
import os, subprocess, sys, tempfile

root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
proj = os.path.join(root, "project")
os.makedirs(os.path.join(proj, "data"))
with open(os.path.join(proj, "data", "input.csv"), "w") as f:
    f.write("a,b\n1,2\n")

PROG = (
    "try:\n"
    "    open('data/input.csv').read()\n"
    "    print('opened data/input.csv')\n"
    "except FileNotFoundError:\n"
    "    print('FileNotFoundError: data/input.csv')\n"
)
for label, cwd in (("cwd = project/", proj), ("cwd = home/", root)):
    out = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", PROG], cwd=cwd,
                         capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(label, "->", out.stdout.strip())

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
cwd = project/ -> opened data/input.csv
cwd = home/ -> FileNotFoundError: data/input.csv

A relative path is not a location — it's directions from wherever the process happens to be standing. 'data/input.csv' means 'a data directory under the current working directory'. Run from the project folder, those directions lead to the real file. The task runner launches the process with a different working directory (often the user's home, or /), and the same directions lead to a data directory that doesn't exist there. FileNotFoundError is the honest result.

The file being 'right there in the project' is a statement about the project; the error is a statement about the process's cwd. Those coincide only when you launch from the project yourself, which is why this bug class survives every manual test and fails every automated launch.

Fixes: resolve data paths relative to something stable — the script's own location (Path(__file__).parent in Python), an explicit base directory from configuration, or an environment variable the launcher sets. Printing os.getcwd() at startup during diagnosis turns this from a mystery into a one-line log entry. And in general: any relative path in code that a scheduler, service manager, or IDE might launch is a latent bug with a timer on it.

I replaced a tool binary with a newer version in the same directory, but my long-running terminal session kept running the old one until I opened a new tab. The file on disk was definitely new. Why did the old session not notice?

Because your shell caches command locations. To avoid searching every PATH directory on every command, bash remembers ('hashes') where it found each command name. When you replaced the binary in place, the file changed but the shell's cached path still pointed at the same location — wait, same path, new contents should just run... unless the binary moved directories, or the replacement was installed to a different directory that also appears in PATH. That second case is the usual one: the new version landed in a directory earlier or later in PATH, and the shell kept using its hashed entry.

Either way, the shell's memory is the stale layer. `hash -r` clears the command hash table and forces fresh lookups; a new tab works because a new shell starts with an empty table. You can inspect the table with `hash` and see the remembered paths and hit counts.

The broader lesson: shells are stateful environments with caches, and 'the file on disk' and 'what this session will execute' are different facts. When a tool behaves like an older version than the one you installed, check `which` and the hash table in that session before doubting the install.

Half our scripts start with #!/usr/bin/env python3 and half with #!/usr/bin/python3. A teammate says the env form is why a script picked up his virtualenv's Python instead of the system one. Is that plausible, and which form should we standardize on?

Completely plausible, and it's the defining difference between the two forms. #!/usr/bin/python3 names an exact interpreter: that file, every time, regardless of context. #!/usr/bin/env python3 asks env to find 'python3' by searching the *current PATH* — so whatever directory comes first wins. In a shell where a virtualenv is activated, the venv's bin directory is first on PATH, and the env form dutifully runs the venv's interpreter. The absolute form ignores the venv entirely.

Neither is universally right; they encode different intentions. The env form says 'run me with the Python this context prefers' — good for portable scripts and development tools that should respect venvs. The absolute form says 'run me with the system Python specifically' — good for system utilities and scheduled jobs that must not change behavior because someone activated an environment.

Standardize by category rather than globally: scripts that are part of a project and live in its venv get the env form; scripts installed as system tooling get the absolute path (or better, an explicit path to the exact venv they belong to). The bug isn't either shebang — it's a script whose shebang expresses the opposite intention from its deployment.

On my laptop `python` runs Python 3 fine. On our server, `python` gives 'command not found' but `python3` works, and a vendor script that starts with #!/usr/bin/env python dies instantly. Is the server's Python broken?

No — the server's Python is fine; the *name* is what's missing. `python` and `python3` are separate command names, and nothing requires both to exist. Many current distributions install only `python3` (plus versioned names like `python3.12`), having retired the unversioned `python` name when Python 2 reached end of life. Your laptop has some package — a python-is-python3 shim, a framework install, a venv — that provides the `python` alias, which makes the difference invisible until you move machines.

The vendor script fails for the same reason: its shebang asks env to find `python`, the lookup fails, and the script never starts. The error message mentions the script, which misleads people into debugging the script.

Practical rules: write `python3` in your own scripts and commands unless you are deliberately inside a venv (where `python` is provided and correct); treat any tool that assumes bare `python` on a modern system as carrying a portability bug; and when a machine 'has Python but scripts can't find it', compare `which python python3` on both boxes before anything else. Names are environment too.
People say 'activate the virtualenv' like it's a mode the shell enters. When I look, all I see is a directory with a python binary in it. What does activation actually change, mechanically?

arguments.code:
import os, shutil, tempfile

root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
bin_dir = os.path.join(root, "venv", "bin")
os.makedirs(bin_dir)
p = os.path.join(bin_dir, "python")
with open(p, "w") as f:
    f.write("#!/bin/sh\necho venv-python\n")
os.chmod(p, 0o755)

def label(found):
    return "venv" if os.sep + "venv" + os.sep in found else "system"

plain = shutil.which("python3", path="/usr/bin:/bin")
with_venv = shutil.which("python", path=bin_dir + ":/usr/bin:/bin")
print("no venv on PATH: python3 ->", label(plain))
print("venv first:      python  ->", label(with_venv))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
no venv on PATH: python3 -> system
venv first:      python  -> venv

Mechanically, activation is two small edits to your shell's environment and nothing more mystical. It prepends the venv's bin directory to PATH, and it sets a variable named VIRTUAL_ENV pointing at the venv. That's essentially the whole trick — plus cosmetic changes like adjusting your prompt and adding a `deactivate` shell function.

The run shows why the PATH edit is the one that matters: with the venv's bin first, the name `python` resolves to the venv's binary; without it, you get the system's. The venv's `python` is a real interpreter (usually a link to one) that knows its own location, and from that location it finds the venv's library directories instead of the system's — which is how the same interpreter binary serves different package sets depending on where it was invoked from.

This demystifies the common failures. A scheduler 'not using the venv' is just a PATH that lacks the venv's bin (fix: call the venv's python by absolute path — activation is a convenience for humans, not a requirement). Two tools disagreeing about which packages exist are usually two different resolutions of the name `python`. And 'deactivate didn't fix it' means some other layer — a shebang, an alias, a cached hash — is still pointing at the venv.

My Python program launches a helper with subprocess and gets FileNotFoundError, even though I can type the helper's name in my terminal and it runs. The helper is definitely on my PATH. Why does subprocess not find what my shell finds?

Because 'my PATH' and 'the PATH your program inherited' are the same only if nothing in between changed it — and because subprocess without shell=True doesn't ask a shell to do the lookup, it performs the search itself against the environment of the Python process. If that process was started by an IDE, a service manager, a scheduler, or a parent script that adjusted the environment, its PATH can be quite different from your interactive shell's.

There's a second, quieter possibility: the name you type in the terminal might not be a PATH lookup at all. Aliases and shell functions intercept names before PATH is consulted. `type helper` in your shell tells you what the name really is there; if it's an alias or function, no subprocess will ever find it, because it exists only inside your shell.

Diagnose inside the failing context, not beside it: have the program print os.environ['PATH'] and shutil.which('helper') at startup, and compare with `which helper` in your terminal. Nine times out of ten the two PATHs differ by exactly the directory that matters. The fix is then mechanical — set the environment where the program is launched, or pass an explicit env with the PATH you intend, or call the helper by absolute path.

After the third 'works interactively, fails from the scheduler' incident, our team lead banned relative paths and bare command names in anything that runs unattended. Is that overkill, or is it the right rule?

It's the right rule, and it's cheaper than it looks. Both bans target the same root cause: a name — whether a command or a file path — is resolved against context (PATH, working directory) that the author doesn't control once a scheduler, service manager, or a different user runs the job. Interactively, the context is yours and stable, so the fragility is invisible. Unattended, the context belongs to the launcher, and it differs.

Absolute paths move the resolution from launch time to authoring time: /opt/tools/bin/zzbackup is the same file no matter who runs it or from where. The cost is real but small — paths are longer, and moving an installation means updating references — and it's paid once, while a context bug is paid per incident, usually at 3 a.m.

Where teams soften the rule sensibly: inside a project, paths relative to the program's own location (derived from the script file's path, not the cwd) are as stable as absolute ones and survive the project moving as a unit. And configuration files can hold the absolute paths so scripts stay readable. What you can't soften away is dependence on the caller's cwd or the caller's PATH. Your lead's ban is really a ban on invisible inputs — and invisible inputs are what 'works on my machine' is made of.
I'm told there might be two versions of our `report` tool installed. `which report` shows one path. How do I see all of them, and how do I know which one a given context will actually run?

`which` stops at the first match, which is the answer to 'what will run' but hides the existence of rivals. Use `type -a report` in bash: it lists every interpretation of the name in resolution order — aliases and functions first, then every PATH directory containing a matching executable, in order. The first executable in that list is what runs; the rest are the rivals waiting for a PATH change to promote them.

To know what a *given context* will run, you have to evaluate the lookup in that context, because PATH is per-process environment. In the scheduler's context that might mean running the job with a diagnostic line, or reproducing its environment (minimal PATH, its working directory, its user) and asking there. `which` in your shell certifies only your shell.

A useful inventory habit on shared boxes: for your critical tool names, run `type -a` once and look at the list with fresh eyes. Duplicate installs — a distro package in /usr/bin, a manual install in /usr/local/bin, a leftover in someone's home bin — are extremely common, and every one of them is a future incident where an upgrade updates one copy and the context keeps executing the other. Consolidating to a single installed copy, or naming versions distinctly, removes the whole class.

Our app reads configuration from defaults, a config file, environment variables, and command-line flags, 'in that order'. A user insists the port they set in the file is being ignored even though the file is definitely loaded. Walk through how the layers combine and where their port went.

arguments.code:
import json, os, tempfile

config = {"host": "localhost", "port": 8000, "debug": False}
print("defaults:      ", config)

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "app.json")
with open(path, "w") as f:
    json.dump({"port": 9000}, f)
with open(path) as f:
    config.update(json.load(f))
print("after file:    ", config)

config.update({"debug": True})   # from APP_DEBUG in the environment
print("after env:     ", config)

config.update({"port": 7000})    # from --port on the command line
print("after CLI args:", config)

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
The layers don't merge democratically — each layer overwrites the keys it mentions, and later layers win. The trace shows the file doing its job: after the file loads, the port is the user's 9000. But the command line is applied after the file, and it carries a port of 7000, so the effective value is 7000. The user's observation 'the file is loaded but my port is ignored' is precisely correct; the file was read and then overridden.

This is the standard precedence — built-in defaults, then config file, then environment, then command line — on the theory that the more specific, more immediate instruction should win. It's a good design, but it makes 'my setting is ignored' ambiguous until you know every layer's contribution. The port could also have been overridden by the environment layer on another machine, which is how this bug travels: same file, same flags, different env, different winner.

The forensic tool for this class is an effective-config dump: at startup, print the final merged configuration (with secrets masked). One glance replaces the whole argument about which layer spoke last. When you build such a system, also consider recording *which* layer supplied each value — it turns the dump from an answer into an explanation.

I edited our service's config file and put a distinctive host value in it to prove whether it's being read. The service still uses its built-in default host. The file is named app.yaml and sits in the config directory. Prove what's happening.

arguments.code:
import os, tempfile

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
with open(os.path.join(d, "app.yaml"), "w") as f:
    f.write("host: SENTINEL-FROM-YAML\n")

loaded = {"host": "default.internal"}
for name in ("app.yml",):  # the loader only ever looks for this name
    p = os.path.join(d, name)
    if os.path.exists(p):
        loaded["host"] = open(p).read().split(": ")[1].strip()

print("files in config dir:", sorted(os.listdir(d)))
print("host the program runs with:", loaded["host"])

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
files in config dir: ['app.yaml']
host the program runs with: default.internal

Your sentinel experiment worked perfectly — it just proved the opposite of what you hoped. The directory contains app.yaml; the loader looks for app.yml; the file is never opened, and the program runs with its built-in default. The distinctive value was a good idea: because SENTINEL-FROM-YAML appears nowhere in the effective config, you know the file wasn't read at all, as opposed to read-and-overridden or read-and-misparsed.

The .yaml/.yml pair is the classic instance — both extensions are in wide use, different tools prefer different ones, and nothing on a filesystem will warn you that you picked the other spelling. The same shape recurs with .ini/.cfg/.conf, with config.json versus settings.json, and with directories (config/ versus conf/).

Generalize your experiment into the standard move for 'my config change has no effect': put a unique sentinel value in the file, restart, and grep the program's effective-config output (or its behavior) for the sentinel. Absent sentinel means the file was never read — then list the directory, compare names character by character, and check which filename the loader actually opens. Present sentinel with a wrong value means it was read and something else is wrong. Two minutes of experiment replaces an hour of rereading the file you edited.

I edited our app's mode file from 'fast' to 'safe' while the app was running, and the app kept behaving as 'fast' until I restarted it — then it picked up 'safe' immediately. A restart 'fixing' it feels like superstition. What's the mechanism?

arguments.code:
import os, tempfile

path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "mode.txt")
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write("fast")

_cache = {}
def get_mode(reload=False):
    if reload or "mode" not in _cache:
        _cache["mode"] = open(path).read()
    return _cache["mode"]

print("first read:          ", get_mode())
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write("safe")
print("after editing file:  ", get_mode())
print("after explicit reload:", get_mode(reload=True))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
first read:           fast
after editing file:   fast
after explicit reload: safe

No superstition — the app cached the value. The first read loaded 'fast' into memory; every later read was served from the cache without touching the file, so your edit changed a file nobody was reading anymore. Restarting emptied the cache, the first read after restart loaded 'safe', and the change 'took'. The third line shows the designed alternative: an explicit reload path that re-reads the file on demand.

Caching configuration is normal and often correct — re-reading a file on every request is wasteful, and some values (a listen port) can't sensibly change mid-flight anyway. The failure is a mismatch of expectations: you believed the file was the live configuration; the program treated it as startup input. Both views are defensible; the incident is that nobody said which one this program implements.

Forensically, 'a restart fixed it' is a strong signal pointing at exactly this: state held in the process — cached config, pooled connections, memoized lookups — that a restart resets. When you see that pattern, ask 'what does this process hold in memory that the outside world thinks it re-reads?' Fixes live on a spectrum: document that the setting is restart-only, add a reload trigger (a signal, an admin endpoint, a file-watch), or read at use time for the few settings that genuinely need to be live.
Every tool we use seems to layer configuration differently. Is there an actual convention for which source wins — defaults, file, environment, command line — or does everyone just make it up?

There's a strong convention, even if individual tools deviate: command line beats environment, environment beats config file, config file beats built-in defaults. The logic is specificity and immediacy — the flag you typed for this one run should outweigh the standing configuration, which should outweigh the author's shipped guesses.

Deviations exist and are worth knowing about. Some tools treat the environment as a fallback below the file, especially older Unix tools where the file is the primary interface. Some merge structured config from several files in a directory (all files in conf.d/, sorted, later overriding earlier). And some settings exist in only one layer — a debug flag that only the command line can set, for safety.

The practical consequences: when a setting 'won't take', enumerate the layers in that tool's documented order and check each one for the key — the winner is often a layer you forgot existed, like an environment variable exported months ago in a profile. When you build a tool, follow the convention, document it in one sentence, and print the effective configuration on request. Most config-precedence pain is not disagreement about the order; it's that the order was never stated and the effective result was never visible.

I edited the app.conf in my home directory and nothing changed. A colleague found another app.conf in /etc and a third in the install directory. How do programs usually choose, and how do I find out which one mine read?

Most programs search a fixed list of locations in order and use the first file that exists. A typical order: a path given explicitly on the command line or in an environment variable, then the current directory or the user's home directory, then a system directory like /etc, then a default bundled with the installation. First match wins — the other files aren't merged, aren't read, and might as well not exist, which is why your home-directory edit was inert: something earlier in the search order (very likely /etc, if the search checks it before home, or the install dir) was found first.

To find out which file yours read, in increasing order of effort: check the documentation or `--help` for the search order and any --config flag or APP_CONFIG-style environment override; put a sentinel value in each candidate and see which sentinel shows up in the effective config; or watch the process open files (strace on Linux, if you have it) and read the answer directly from the syscalls.

Two hygiene rules prevent the whole genre: keep exactly one live copy of a config file and delete or clearly rename the spares (app.conf.disabled), because a dormant config file is a trap for the next editor; and prefer launching with an explicit --config path in service definitions, so the question 'which file?' has a one-word answer.

Our deployment sets APP_DATABASE_HOST and APP_DATABASE_PORT in the environment, and the app still connects to localhost. The app reads its database settings from the environment — I checked the code myself. Where's the disconnect?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
effective config: {'db_host': 'localhost', 'db_port': '5432'}
set but never read: ['APP_DATABASE_HOST', 'APP_DATABASE_PORT']

In the mapping between the two naming schemes. The deployment sets APP_DATABASE_HOST; the code looks up APP_DB_HOST. Both sides are 'reading the environment' and both sides are internally consistent — they just disagree about the variable's name, so every lookup misses and every default quietly applies. The last line of the run is the smoking gun: the environment contains variables that no code path ever reads.

This happens wherever two conventions meet: one team's APP_DATABASE_* prefix against another's APP_DB_*, or a framework's naming scheme against an operator's. Because environment lookups with defaults fail silently, the system runs — on localhost, against a dev database, with default pool sizes — and the mismatch can survive for a long time if the defaults happen to work.

Catching it: compare the set of variable names present in the environment against the set the program reads, and investigate both differences — read-but-unset (usually loud or defaulted) and set-but-unread (always silent, always suspicious). Preventing it: publish the exact variable names in the deployment docs next to the values, and have the program log, at startup, the names it consulted and which were found. A name is an interface; treat a rename like an API break.

'Just restart it' fixes a depressing number of our config issues. Management wants fewer restarts. Which kinds of settings fundamentally need one, and which only need one because of how the code happens to be written?

Very few settings fundamentally need a restart; most need one because the value was read once and stored. Sort settings into three kinds. Continuous settings — log verbosity, feature flags, sampling rates — are read at use time or through a reloadable holder in well-built systems and can change live with no restart at all. Session settings — timeouts, pool sizes, retry counts — are typically captured when a component is constructed; changing them live means rebuilding that component, which good frameworks support and ad-hoc code usually doesn't. Structural settings — the listen port, the database it points at, the identity it runs as — are woven into sockets, connections, and credentials that are genuinely awkward to swap mid-flight; a restart (or a rolling replacement of the process) is the honest mechanism there.

So the management goal is achievable but it's engineering work, not policy: identify which settings operators actually change, move them from the 'read once at import' pile into an explicit configuration object with a reload path (signal, admin endpoint, file watch), and leave structural settings restart-only on purpose, documented as such.

Until then, keep restarting without guilt — but notice the pattern. 'Restart fixed it' tells you the process held stale state; logging which state that was, each time, builds the list of what to make reloadable first.

I read APP_PORT from the environment in Python, and later `port + 1` crashes with a TypeError about concatenating str and int. The environment clearly says 8080, which is a number. Why does Python think it's a string?

arguments.code:
import os
os.environ["APP_PORT"] = "8080"
port = os.environ["APP_PORT"]
print("type read from env:", type(port).__name__, "value:", port)
try:
    port + 1
except TypeError as e:
    print("port + 1 ->", type(e).__name__ + ":", e)
print("after int():", int(port) + 1)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
type read from env: str value: 8080
port + 1 -> TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
after int(): 8081

Because the environment has no numbers — it has only strings. Every variable in a process environment is text: names are text, values are text. When you write 8080 in a config file or a unit, what's stored is the four characters '8080'. os.environ faithfully returns those characters as a str, and '8080' + 1 is string-plus-int, which Python refuses.

The value 'clearly being a number' is a human reading. To the runtime it's a string that happens to contain only digits, exactly like '0808' or '8080 ' (with a trailing space, another classic) — both of which int() handles differently than naive code expects.

The discipline this implies: parse at the boundary. The moment a value enters your program from the environment, a file, or the network, convert it to its real type — int(port), float(rate), an explicit boolean parse — and let the conversion failure happen there, at startup, with the variable's name in the error message. Code that sprinkles int() at every use site, or worse, relies on values 'looking numeric', is deferring a type error to a random Tuesday. Configuration parsing is a real layer of the program; give it the same care as parsing user input, because that's what it is.

We fixed a config value in the repo, merged, deployed — and production kept the old value. Turns out the deployed package bundles a copy of the config from build time. Is bundling config with the artifact ever right, and how should we have caught this?

Bundling *defaults* with the artifact is right and common; bundling the *operative* configuration is how you get this incident. The distinction: values that are part of the program's logic (a default timeout, the shape of a retry policy) travel with the code and version with it. Values that describe the deployment (hosts, ports, credentials, region, sizes) belong to the environment the artifact lands in, and baking them in at build time means 'deploying a config change' silently requires a rebuild nobody knows about — exactly your story: the repo was fixed, the deploy succeeded, and the running value came from a file frozen at build time.

You'd have caught it with the sentinel test: put a distinctive value in the repo config, deploy, and check the effective config the process reports. If the sentinel isn't there, the running config isn't coming from where you think. You'd also have caught it by asking the build one question — 'list every config file inside the artifact' — and reviewing the list with fresh eyes.

The structural fix: the artifact should contain at most example/default configuration, clearly named (config.example.yaml), with the real configuration supplied at deploy time from the environment's own store, and the effective-config dump at startup stating which file (or 'built-in defaults') each value came from. Then 'where does production's value come from?' is a question with a log line for an answer.
A senior engineer keeps saying 'use a sentinel value' when we argue about whether a config file is being read. What is the technique, exactly, and what does each outcome prove?

The technique: instead of editing a config value to the value you want and checking whether behavior changes — a test with many possible explanations — you set the value to something unique, unmistakable, and otherwise impossible, like host = SENTINEL-7f3a9, restart, and look for the sentinel in the program's observable behavior: its effective-config dump, its logs, the error message when it tries to connect to a host named SENTINEL-7f3a9.

Each outcome eliminates a branch of the search tree. Sentinel appears: the file *is* read, so your problem is downstream — parsing, precedence, a later layer overriding it. Sentinel absent and the old value still in effect: either the file is not the one being read (wrong name, wrong directory, earlier file in the search order) or the value is cached from before. Sentinel absent and the *default* in effect: the file was never opened, which points at name/path/search-order, full stop.

What makes it powerful is that it converts an argument about intentions ('I edited the right file, I'm sure') into an observation. It works for environment variables (set one to a sentinel and see if the program reports it), for PATH questions (a sentinel executable that prints its name), and for deployment pipelines (a sentinel in the artifact that should appear in the deployment). Whenever a configuration dispute lasts more than a few minutes, stop debating and plant a sentinel.

We vendored a tiny `greeter` helper into two services at different times. Service A prints friendly greetings; service B, using 'the same' greeter.py, rejects half the inputs. Nobody changed the call sites. Show how the same import can load different code, and how you'd prove which copy a process loaded.

arguments.code:
import os, subprocess, sys, tempfile

root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for ver, msg in (("v1", "hello from v1"), ("v2", "hello from v2 (stricter)")):
    d = os.path.join(root, ver)
    os.makedirs(d)
    with open(os.path.join(d, "greeter.py"), "w") as f:
        f.write(f"def greet():\n    return {msg!r}\n")

PROG = ("import greeter, os\n"
        "print(os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(greeter.__file__)), '->', greeter.greet())\n")
for ver in ("v1", "v2"):
    env = dict(os.environ, PYTHONPATH=os.path.join(root, ver))
    out = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", PROG], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True)
    print("PYTHONPATH=" + ver + ":", out.stdout.strip())

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
PYTHONPATH=v1: v1 -> hello from v1
PYTHONPATH=v2: v2 -> hello from v2 (stricter)

An import statement names a module, not a file. Which file satisfies the name is decided at runtime by the search path — sys.path, built from PYTHONPATH, the script's directory, and the installed library locations, in that order. The run puts two different greeter.py files at the front of the path in turn, and the identical `import greeter` loads v1 in one process and v2 in the other. Service B didn't get different call sites; it got a different copy of the callee.

Vendored copies drift exactly this way: copied at different times, patched in one place, and invisible because the name — the thing everyone checks — never changed.

The proof technique is in the demo: print module.__file__ (and any __version__ the module offers) at startup or in the diagnostic path. 'Which greeter are you?' is a question the process can answer definitively, and the answer is a path, not an opinion. Prevention is structural: vendor once, in one shared package with a version, or stop vendoring and depend on the library properly. But even then, keep the __file__ print in your toolbox — the same technique settles 'which config', 'which binary', and 'which library version' disputes of every flavor.

Our codebase is full of checks like `if python_version >= (3, 9): use the new API`. A reviewer wants them replaced with try/except and hasattr checks. Who's right, and does it matter for surviving version drift?

The reviewer is mostly right, and the reason is exactly about drift. A version check encodes a claim about the world — 'the new API exists in 3.9 and later' — that can be wrong in both directions: a distribution may backport the API into an older series, a newer version may remove or rename it, and a different implementation may not share the numbering at all. When the claim is wrong, the check picks the wrong branch while looking perfectly reasonable.

Feature detection asks the environment directly: try the import and fall back on ImportError, or branch on hasattr(module, 'new_thing'). The answer comes from the actual runtime in front of you, so backports, removals, and alternative implementations are all handled by observation rather than by a table of claims. This is the same forensic instinct as printing module.__file__: prefer measuring the environment to assuming it.

Version checks still have legitimate uses: working around a *bug* that exists in specific versions (where the feature exists but misbehaves), gating behavior that changed semantics without changing any name, and supporting windows where you must reject ancient runtimes outright. Even there, a comment naming the bug is essential, because the check is a claim about history.

Rule of thumb: detect features when you need a capability; check versions when you're avoiding a known defect — and expect feature detection to survive the next upgrade quietly while version tables quietly rot.

A monitoring script of ours parses Python exception messages as strings — it looks for a key name inside KeyError text. It broke after a Python upgrade even though the code raising the error didn't change. Why are exception messages an unstable interface across versions?

Because a message is a human-readable rendering, and Python explicitly reserves the right to improve renderings between versions. The KeyError case is the cleanest example: str(KeyError('user_id')) is "'user_id'" — the repr of the key, quotes included. Code that strips quotes, splits on them, or pattern-matches the message is coupled to that rendering choice. When a version changes how a message is phrased, quoted, or punctuated — and minor versions do this regularly, for exceptions, for warnings, for error hints — the parser breaks even though the exception type, its args, and the raising code are all identical.

The stable interface is the structured data: the exception's type, and its args. KeyError stores the key in e.args[0]; FileNotFoundError exposes .filename and .errno; subprocess errors carry .returncode and .output. Programs should branch on those, and reserve message text for humans and logs.

This generalizes past exceptions: any string meant for people — CLI output, log lines, --version banners — is a rendering, not an API, and parsing it builds your system on a surface that its owners feel free to polish. When you catch yourself writing a regex against another program's prose, stop and look for the structured channel: an attribute, an exit code, a JSON mode, an environment variable. There almost always is one, and it's the one that survives upgrades.

Our requirements file says `requests>=2.28` and production ended up with a requests version two years newer than what I developed against. I thought I'd 'pinned' it. What do the different specifiers actually promise?

`requests>=2.28` promises only a floor: any version from 2.28 upward satisfies it, including next year's 2.40 with whatever behavior it brings. That's not a pin; it's a minimum. The specifiers, from loosest to strictest: `>=2.28` (floor only), `~=2.28` (compatible release: >=2.28, <2.29's next major boundary — effectively the 2.x line at or above 2.28... precisely, <3.0 for ~=2.28 with two components), `>=2.28,<3` (an explicit window), and `==2.31.0` (an exact pin, the only form that names one version).

But even an exact pin on your direct dependencies doesn't freeze the environment, because your dependencies have dependencies. Transitive packages float according to *their* specifiers unless something records the full resolved set. That record is a lockfile (or a complete pip freeze): every package, direct and transitive, at an exact version, ideally with hashes.

The working arrangement most teams land on: requirements express intent with sane windows; a lockfile, generated and committed, expresses the exact tested set; deployments install from the lockfile; development upgrades regenerate it deliberately. Your incident is the gap between the first and the second — intent was recorded, the tested set wasn't, and production resolved the intent fresh, two years later, into a different environment.

After upgrading a server from Python 3.9 to 3.12, our app fails at startup with an import error for `from collections import Mapping`, which worked for years. The code didn't change. What happened, and what's the durable fix?

arguments.code:
try:
    from collections import Mapping
    print("from collections import Mapping: OK")
except ImportError:
    print("from collections import Mapping: ImportError")

from collections.abc import Mapping as Mapping2
print("from collections.abc import Mapping: OK ->", Mapping2.__name__)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
from collections import Mapping: ImportError
from collections.abc import Mapping: OK -> Mapping

The standard library moved the name and eventually removed the forwarding address. The abstract base classes (Mapping, Sequence, Iterable, and friends) have lived in collections.abc since Python 3.3; for years, importing them from collections itself also worked, as a deprecated alias. Python 3.10 removed the aliases, so on 3.12 the old import is simply an ImportError. Your code didn't change; the environment's contract did, across a boundary you crossed in the upgrade.

The durable fix is to import from the canonical location, collections.abc — correct on every Python from 3.3 through today, so the fixed code runs on both the old and new interpreters. During a migration, a try/except that attempts the new location first and falls back to the old is the standard bridge.

The broader pattern is worth naming: deprecations are version drift on a schedule. The alias worked for *seven years* while emitting (or eligible to emit) deprecation warnings, and the removal still arrived as a surprise because warnings nobody reads are indistinguishable from silence. When you upgrade an interpreter, run the test suite with warnings visible (`python -W default`) on the *old* version first — the removals in the next version are usually announced, in writing, in the current one's warnings.

Two machines installed from the same requirements.txt a month apart run different versions of a transitive dependency, and one of them has a bug the other doesn't. Nobody edited requirements.txt. How is that possible, and what artifact would have prevented it?

Because requirements.txt, as most teams write it, specifies direct dependencies with ranges — and a range is re-resolved every time someone installs. The resolver picks the newest versions satisfying all constraints *on the day of the install*. A month apart means a month of new releases: the transitive dependency (a dependency of something you depend on, which you may never have named) moved, and the second machine resolved to it. Same file, same command, different environment — version drift through the calendar.

The artifact that prevents it is a lockfile: the complete, exact output of one resolution — every package, direct and transitive, with exact versions (and ideally hashes) — committed alongside requirements.txt. Installs then reproduce that set instead of re-solving the puzzle. pip's equivalent is a fully pinned `pip freeze` output used as the install source; modern tools (pip-tools, uv, Poetry, PDM) generate and maintain lockfiles as a first-class step.

The forensic habit that pairs with it: when two machines disagree, diff their *installed* sets (`pip freeze` on both, then diff) rather than their requirements files. The requirements are the intent; the freeze is the fact. Incidents live in the gap between them.
Our report generator prints section names in different orders on different runs of the same code on the same machine. Someone blamed 'hash randomization'. Is that a real mechanism, or an excuse?

It's a real mechanism, and it's deliberately there. Python randomizes the hash values of strings (and bytes) per process, using a seed drawn at startup, as a defense against hash-collision denial-of-service attacks. Anything whose iteration order depends on hash values — sets most visibly, and dicts built in hash-dependent ways in old code — can therefore enumerate in a different order in every new process, even with identical code, identical input, and an identical machine.

Your report generator is almost certainly collecting section names in a set (or deduplicating through one) and printing them in set order. The order was never promised; it just happened to look stable in whatever runs someone eyeballed.

You can prove the mechanism rather than argue about it: run the interpreter twice with the PYTHONHASHSEED environment variable set to two different fixed values and watch the order change deterministically per seed; set it to the same value twice and the order repeats. That experiment converts folklore into evidence.

The fix is not to disable randomization (you'd be reopening the security hole to preserve a coincidence). The fix is to never let output order depend on hash order: sort at the point of presentation, or keep insertion-ordered structures (dict preserves insertion order as a language guarantee) when order matters. Treat set iteration order as unspecified — because it is.

A script runs fine when I invoke the venv's python directly, but a colleague runs 'the same venv' and gets different package behavior. Turned out her venv was created with Python 3.11 and mine with 3.12. Can a venv's origin Python cause real differences like that?

Yes, in two distinct ways. First, the language itself: a venv is not a container for an interpreter — it's a directory structure bound to the interpreter that created it, and its `python` is (usually) a link to that base interpreter. A 3.11 venv runs Python 3.11 forever, with 3.11's standard library, syntax, and behavior, no matter what else is installed around it. If your code uses a 3.12-only stdlib location or syntax, hers fails or falls back differently, while both of you truthfully say 'I used the venv'.

Second, the packages: wheels are built per interpreter version. A package installed into a 3.11 venv is the 3.11 build of it; compiled extensions differ, and occasionally a package's pure-Python code branches on sys.version_info. So even 'the same package version' is not byte-identical across the two venvs.

The checks are quick: `python -VV` (or the venv's pyvenv.cfg, which records the base interpreter's path and version) tells you what a venv really is. Teams that ship venvs around — or recreate them from scripts — should record the creating interpreter's version next to the requirements, because 'Python 3' is not an environment specification; 'CPython 3.12.3' is.

Our input validation is done with assert statements, and it works in development. In production the same invalid inputs sail through. The only difference anyone can name is that production launches Python with the -O flag. Demonstrate the mechanism.

arguments.code:
import subprocess, sys

PROG = (
    "def check_port(p):\n"
    "    assert 0 < p < 65536, 'port out of range'\n"
    "    return 'accepted'\n"
    "try:\n"
    "    print(check_port(99999))\n"
    "except AssertionError as e:\n"
    "    print('AssertionError:', e)\n"
)
for args in ([], ["-O"]):
    out = subprocess.run([sys.executable, *args, "-c", PROG],
                         capture_output=True, text=True)
    print("python", " ".join(args) or "(normal)", "->", out.stdout.strip())

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
python (normal) -> AssertionError: port out of range
python -O -> accepted

The run shows it exactly: without flags, the assert fires and the invalid port is rejected; with -O, the same code prints 'accepted'. Python's -O (optimize) flag removes assert statements from the compiled bytecode entirely — they don't evaluate to False, they cease to exist. Production didn't get a different validation result; it got no validation.

This is environment drift in its purest form: identical source, identical input, and a launch flag — a property of how the process was started, invisible in the code — changes the program's meaning. It's also why asserts are for invariants during development (conditions that indicate a programming error if violated), never for validating external input, enforcing security checks, or anything else the program needs in order to be correct.

The fixes: replace input-validation asserts with explicit `if not condition: raise ValueError(...)`, which no flag can remove; and audit launch configuration — flags, environment, working directory — as part of the environment you capture when comparing 'works here, fails there'. A one-character flag in a systemd unit or a Dockerfile CMD line is as much a part of the program's behavior as any line of its source.

We upgraded a library and a subtle behavior changed somewhere in a range of twelve versions. Reading twelve changelogs sounds miserable. Is there a systematic way to find the version where it changed?

Yes — bisect the versions the way you'd bisect commits. You have a known-good version and a known-bad version and a test (even a scrappy script) that prints PASS or FAIL for the behavior in question. Install the version halfway between, run the test, and keep the half that still brackets the change. Twelve versions take about four iterations (log2 of 12) instead of twelve changelog reads, and each iteration is mechanical: install version X into a scratch venv, run the check, record the verdict.

Two things make it work well. First, automate the check before you start — a test you run by eyeballing output will drift; a script that exits 0 or 1 won't. Second, once you've found the boundary version, *then* read exactly one changelog: the one for that release, which will usually name the change and often the reasoning and the migration path.

The same bracketing instinct applies to every 'something in the environment changed' mystery: interpreter versions, dependency versions, OS images, configuration revisions. Halving a search space beats reading it linearly, and the discipline of a repeatable PASS/FAIL check is the same discipline as minimizing a reproduction. You're not looking for the change by reading; you're cornering it by measurement.

Our app was developed on macOS and opens its config as 'config.json'. On the Linux server it crashes with FileNotFoundError, but when I list the directory, the config file is plainly there. Same filename, as far as I can tell. What's the difference?

arguments.code:
import os, tempfile

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
with open(os.path.join(d, "Config.json"), "w") as f:
    f.write("{}")

try:
    open(os.path.join(d, "config.json"))
    print("open('config.json'): OK")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("open('config.json'): FileNotFoundError")
names = os.listdir(d)
print("files present:", names)
print("case-insensitive match:", [n for n in names if n.casefold() == "config.json"])

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
open('config.json'): FileNotFoundError
files present: ['Config.json']
case-insensitive match: ['Config.json']

The filename on disk is Config.json, with a capital C, and on Linux that is a different name from config.json. Linux filesystems are case-sensitive: names are compared byte for byte, so the open fails even though a human reads the directory listing and sees 'the config file'. The last line is the forensic move — comparing case-insensitively finds the near-match that the byte-exact lookup missed.

Your Mac hid this because the default macOS filesystem is case-insensitive (case-preserving): it stores 'Config.json' but happily answers lookups for 'config.json'. Windows behaves the same way. So the code 'worked' for its entire development life on an environment that forgave the mismatch, and Linux — which forgives nothing — is where the latent bug became visible. Neither box is wrong; they implement different name rules.

Fixes and habits: make the on-disk name and the code agree exactly (and rename in version control carefully — some tools need a two-step rename to register a case-only change); when a file is 'plainly there' but won't open, list the directory programmatically and compare names byte-wise or casefolded, rather than by eye; and treat any filename that differs from another only by case as a hazard in its own right, since it cannot even exist on the forgiving filesystems.

An API token read from a file keeps failing authentication in Python, but the same token pasted into curl works. The token in the file looks identical to what I paste. I compared them visually a dozen times. What invisible thing should I look for?

arguments.code:
line = b"token=abc123\r\n".decode().split("\n")[0]
value = line.split("=", 1)[1]
print("parsed value repr:", repr(value))
print("equals 'abc123'?", value == "abc123")
print("after strip:     ", value.strip() == "abc123")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
parsed value repr: 'abc123\r'
equals 'abc123'? False
after strip:      True

A carriage return. The file has Windows line endings (CRLF), and the parsing here split on '\n' only, so the '\r' stayed attached to the end of the token: the parsed value is 'abc123\r', which is not equal to 'abc123' no matter how identical they look on screen. The server receives a token with an extra control character and rejects it; curl works because when you paste, you paste the visible characters only.

The repr() output is the whole diagnosis — it's the tool that makes the invisible visible. Whenever a string comparison fails 'for no reason', stop comparing visually and print repr() of both sides (or their lengths, or a hex dump). Trailing whitespace, a carriage return, a non-breaking space, a BOM at the start of the file: all of them are invisible in a terminal and obvious in a repr.

Where did the \r come from? The file was written or edited on Windows, or by a tool configured for CRLF, or generated by a script that explicitly wrote \r\n — and the reader was written assuming Unix endings. Robust readers strip values from config-like files (value.strip() handles \r, \n, and spaces together), and robust comparisons in debugging always go through repr first. The bug class is 'bytes are not what they appear to be', and repr is its natural predator.

Our app runs as user 'app' and reads its config fine. The nightly job runs as user 'svc' and gets permission denied on the secrets file, but can read the regular config in the same directory. Both files are 'there'. Walk me through the permission arithmetic.

arguments.code:
import os, stat, tempfile

d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for name, mode in (("app.conf", 0o644), ("secrets.conf", 0o600)):
    p = os.path.join(d, name)
    open(p, "w").close()
    os.chmod(p, mode)
    bits = stat.S_IMODE(os.stat(p).st_mode)
    print(f"{name}: {oct(bits)}  owner-read={bool(bits & 0o400)}  "
          f"group-read={bool(bits & 0o040)}  other-read={bool(bits & 0o004)}")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
app.conf: 0o644  owner-read=True  group-read=True  other-read=True
secrets.conf: 0o600  owner-read=True  group-read=False  other-read=False

Permissions are three sets of bits — owner, group, other — and which set applies to a process depends on who the process runs as, not on where the file sits. app.conf is 644: the owner can read and write, and group and *other* can read, so any account on the box, including svc, can read it. secrets.conf is 600: only the owner (app) can read it. When the svc job tries, it falls in the 'other' class for that file, the other-read bit is 0, and the kernel returns permission denied. Same directory, same existence — different arithmetic per reader.

This is why 'the file is there and readable' is an incomplete report: readable *by whom* is the operative question, and the answer changes with the process's user and groups. Services, schedulers, and containers routinely run as different identities than the developer who placed the files.

Diagnose as the failing identity when you can (sudo -u svc cat the file), and read the bits with ls -l or stat rather than guessing. Fix at the right layer: if svc legitimately needs the secrets, the usual answer is a shared group with group-read (640, group set to a group both accounts belong to) — not chmod 644, which hands the secrets to every account on the machine to solve a two-account problem.

A config value kept comparing wrong in our app — 'east' wouldn't match 'east'. It turned out the value in the file had a trailing space that someone typed months ago. Is defensive stripping of every config value the answer, or is that hiding real problems?

Strip, but strip knowingly. For the overwhelming majority of configuration values — hostnames, region names, tokens, paths, enum-like words — surrounding whitespace is never meaningful; it's an artifact of hand-editing, copy-paste, or a file format that pads fields. Normalizing it away at parse time (value.strip() for string settings) removes an entire class of invisible-character bugs at the exact boundary where the value enters the program, and your 'east ' incident is the class's poster child.

The honest caveat: whitespace *is* meaningful in a few places — passwords can legitimately contain leading or trailing spaces, literal text blocks, format strings. A blanket strip applied to secret values has bitten real systems (the stored password and the typed password get stripped differently by different components). So the refined rule is: strip by default for structural values, and don't strip values whose content is opaque user data — passwords, keys, free text — where instead you should compare and store byte-exactly and debug mismatches with repr().

Either way, the deeper fix is at the boundary: parse configuration once, into typed, normalized values, and let the rest of the program never see the raw text. If 'east ' can reach a comparison deep in the app, the parser abdicated. And when a comparison fails mysteriously anywhere, repr() both sides before theorizing — the trailing space confesses immediately.

A user of my tool passed an absolute path as the 'filename' setting, and my code's os.path.join(base_dir, filename) silently produced a path outside base_dir entirely. I thought join always prepends. Show me what it actually does.

arguments.code:
import os
print(os.path.join("/srv/app", "data.txt"))
print(os.path.join("/srv/app", "/etc/other.txt"))
base = "/srv/app"
user_supplied = "/etc/other.txt"
print("joined with user path:", os.path.join(base, user_supplied))
print("stays under base:", os.path.join(base, user_supplied).startswith(base))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
/srv/app/data.txt
/etc/other.txt
joined with user path: /etc/other.txt
stays under base: False

join doesn't prepend — it concatenates path components *unless* a later component is absolute, in which case everything before it is discarded. With 'data.txt' you get the expected /srv/app/data.txt. With '/etc/other.txt', the leading slash makes it absolute, join throws away /srv/app entirely, and the result is exactly the user's path. No warning, no error: the function is documented to do this.

This bites anywhere a base directory is treated as a safety boundary: upload handlers joining a storage dir with a client-supplied name, config loaders joining a config dir with a setting, extractors joining a target dir with archive member names. An absolute component — or, on some paths, a '..' sequence, which join also passes through untouched — escapes the boundary while the code reads as if it's confining.

The correct pattern is join, then verify: normalize the result (os.path.realpath or Path.resolve) and check it still starts with the normalized base, rejecting it if not. Treat any path that comes from configuration or a user as untrusted input that must be confined, not as a polite suggestion. 'It worked in my tests' means only that your tests never supplied an absolute path — the environment of the test, once again, was narrower than the environment of the world.

On the server, /etc/app/app.conf is a symlink to a file in our deployment directory. I edited the file in the deployment directory and the app picked it up — but last month a deploy 'replaced' the config and my edits vanished, even though the deployment directory file still has them. What are the moving parts here?

There are three objects, not one: the symlink at /etc/app/app.conf, its target in the deployment directory, and whatever the deploy process does. Reading through the symlink, the app sees the target's current content — which is why your edit worked. But deploys commonly replace files atomically by writing a new file and renaming it over the old one, and rename replaces the *directory entry it lands on*. If the deploy wrote to /etc/app/app.conf's location, it replaced the symlink itself with a regular file — the app now reads the deploy's copy, and the deployment-directory file (with your edits) is orphaned: still there, still correct-looking, connected to nothing. The reverse also happens: a deploy that follows the symlink overwrites the shared target, changing every app that links to it.
